posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
I'm kind of bogged down with work at the moment, but regarding the "moisture content of the emulsion" I think it's well-known that a final DCG layer should be quite dry prior to sealing. According to Rallison, if moisture is sealed in, then the hologram might have irregular color-shifts over time. Also, Jeff Blyth has indicated that a very dry DCG layer doesn't really need sealing at all. (But in my case I would seal it anyway to protect it from water-droplets, and just to be on the safe side.) I can confirm this, as I have an old DCG hologram (of some coins) that I didn't seal, and it has been stored in my damp basement for a long time, without any adverse effect. (The kind of dryness that Jeff was referring to was leaving the DCG hologram in a desiccator for a number of days.) 

Really there is a lot of stuff in the literature reagrding the questions you raised, Tony, and it would be quite a project to really get into it. The most valuable information is from fellow DCG holographers.

I don't think it is necessarily true that you lose brightness when compensating as you express.

You have to think about what brightness is. Take for example making a master and making a hologram for viewing. The master would like to be very narrow banded tuned to the wavelength you are shooting thus making a very bright and clean replay in the laser. On the other hand, a viewable hologram can be very broadband and look extreemly bright but may not perform so well as a master. 

If you are trying to get the brightest reflection hologram try for a broadband hologram. I would have to say the holograms that "look" the brightest to me are the broadband gold/yellow holograms. Even though common sense says a white hologram should replay brighter in white light, I personally don't see it. I think it may have something to do with the wavelengths of light. Blue is a pretty dark color and to get white you have to add this blue. But the gold/yellow hologram replay all from green to red and they just seem brighter to me. 

Also, my brightest DCG hologram have always been from H1transmissions. I've gotten real close with SBR but never got that WOW brightness as I did with H1 tranmssions. But I will say most of my SBR DCG holograms are brighter then most H2 silver halide holograms, mostly due to bandwidth I believe.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
I suppose "dissolve" would be technically correct, but since gelatin molecules are so long and threadlike, the word "disperse" would also be good. Of course, ordinary gelatin won't dissolve (and form a clear liquid) until it's heated.

I find it unnecessary to soak the gelatin overnight. However, I do find it important to thoroughly mix the gelatin in cold water (I use magnetic stirring) before turning on the heat. Maybe the term "disperse" would apply to this stage. (On a side note, my 3-30-200 mixture has such a high gelatin content, that my magnetic stirrer can't handle it, even though it's powerful, and I use a large "star" spin bar. I use a plastic spoon for manual mixing, until all the gelatin is thoroughly wetted.)

After all the gelatin is wetted, and there are no clumps of dry powder, I place the mixture in a water bath on top of the hot plate/stirrer, and turn on the heat (thermostatted) with constant stirring. At first my spin bar can't handle the viscosity, and wobbles in an uncontrolled way, but as the gelatin in the bottom of the beaker begins to melt (i.e., completely dissolve) is can start to turn normally.

Martin,

I am curious about the proper terminology, to me dissolve means to dis-associate the ions like adding salt to water. Where as disperse means to evenly distribute small particles into a liquid. At my day job I use a product called Isinglass. It is the swim bladders of tropical fish. It is mainly collagen and my task is to disperse it as finely as possible. I have to mix it throughly with water then acidify it to where the protein does not want to stick and then mix it some more. This process is described in the literature as dispersion since the protein molecules are the same before and after they are just not stuck together. posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
Science semantics 

OK so to me cook would mean something like the browning reaction which we clearly don't want to do. Or polymerization like egg whites which is bad. I think heating just straightens the bonds so they un-tangle and disperse better. The only reason I bring it up is perhaps we can improve the process if we dissect exactly what happens.

As far as dissolve goes, the difference is if you take a cup of sugar you can put almost a cup of hot water in without changing the volume if you slowly stir. If you are only dispersing the volume is additive.

With isenglass the pH is critical to dispersion. There are still photographers who make film from isenglass. I talked to someone from England who was doing it but he was at work and did not have much time. It should work just fine. It is simply the highest quality geletin you can buy. It is hydrated overnight then blended, the pH is adjusted then it is diluted. Once the solution is prepared you add it to the beer by injecting is slowly during a transfer. I add 2 gallons in 20 minutes. The beer settles perfectly clear at about the rate of 1 foot of depth per hour. I do no filtration.
